messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus Chen was fifty-three when the assault happened—a Tuesday evening in late September at a hotel gym in Portland, where he'd been attending a social work conference. He'd gone down after dinner, alone, around nine o'clock. The locker room was empty. A man came in behind him, locked the door, and what followed was a blur of violence and violation that Marcus's mind still refused to fully cohere into language. He remembered the weight, the hands, the feeling of being unmade. He remembered thinking he was going to die. When it ended, he sat alone on the locker room bench for nearly an hour, unable to move, unable to think of anything except that he needed to leave without anyone seeing him.

For the first few weeks, Marcus told almost no one. He told his wife, Jennifer, because he had to, and the words came out fractured and incomplete—he knew what had happened, but something in him could not seem to find the language to describe it, even to her. When he tried to speak about it directly, shame flooded through him so violently that he would go silent. The shame was different from the terror, though they lived together now. The terror was the feeling of being trapped again; the shame was the conviction that he should have fought harder, that something about him had invited this, that he was fundamentally broken. When memories surfaced—unbidden, in the shower, in a meeting, while driving—they came with both sensations at once, the body remembering the panic and the mind flooding with the conviction that he was somehow culpable.

The terror and shame made him want to push the memories away entirely. He tried to suppress them, to force them out of his mind the moment they appeared, but the effort itself seemed to keep them closer, more insistent. He found himself ruminating instead about revenge, about how he might find the man, about scenarios of confrontation and retaliation that he knew were fantasies but which occupied hours of his thinking. These revenge fantasies felt safer than the memories themselves—they gave him a sense of agency, of power, even though they were hollow.

Within weeks, Marcus began to notice that the world had become a place of hidden threats. The assault had happened in an enclosed space, and now enclosed spaces—elevators, locker rooms, even the bathroom at home with the door closed—triggered a suffocating dread. He started checking behind him constantly, especially in parking lots and on walks around the neighborhood. When he was driving, he would glance repeatedly in his mirrors, convinced that someone was following him. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely; he couldn't assess the danger in them, and the uncertainty itself felt unbearable. At work, where he'd spent twenty years counseling clients with trauma, he found himself unable to attend a mandatory training at a new office building downtown. He told his supervisor it was a scheduling conflict.

The hypervigilance fed back into the memories. When he was checking behind him, his body would tense, his heart would accelerate, and suddenly he was back in that locker room, that same helplessness blooming in his chest. The memories and the threat-checking had become inseparable. His attempts to suppress the memories only seemed to sharpen them, to make them more vivid when they broke through. And when he tried to avoid the threat—the checking, the avoidance of unfamiliar places, the refusal to go anywhere enclosed without Jennifer—he would feel a temporary relief that quickly curdled into a sense of his world shrinking. He stopped going to the gym entirely. He declined a promotion that would have required travel. He began to avoid the very spaces and activities that had once given him a sense of competence and freedom.

It was Jennifer who finally insisted he seek help, after finding him in the kitchen at two in the morning, unable to sleep, unable to explain why he was awake except that he'd been lying in bed thinking about the assault and the revenge he'd never enact and whether he would ever feel safe again. He came to his first appointment looking exhausted, his shoulders curved inward, and when the therapist asked him to describe what had brought him in, Marcus fell silent for a long time before saying, very quietly, that he was afraid he was disappearing—not dying, but becoming smaller and smaller, until there would be nothing left of who he used to be.
